title: Norse Greenland
capsule: Erik the Red established the Norse Eastern Settlement on Greenland's southwest coast around 985 CE after his banishment from Iceland; the Western Settlement, some 500 km further north near modern Nuuk, followed shortly after. At its peak in the eleventh to twelfth centuries, the Norse population numbered roughly 2,000–3,000 in some 300 farms, sustaining a pastoral economy and exporting walrus ivory, furs, and live polar bears to Europe. The colonies maintained their own bishopric at Gardar from 1124 and appear in the historical record through the mid-fifteenth century, with the last documented ship voyage recorded in 1408; the cause of their disappearance—attributed to climate deterioration (the Little Ice Age), economic marginalisation as elephant ivory undercut walrus ivory prices, and possibly conflict with expanding Inuit (Thule) populations—remains debated.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Farm sites are archaeologically well located; the geographic boundaries of Norse territory versus Inuit occupation zones in the dataset window (1072–1385) are reasonably attested by medieval saga and archival sources, though the Western Settlement's abandonment date (~1350) carries some uncertainty.
